lead: This unit is the toolkit of named probability models used in engineering, quality control, queues and reliability. You learn when a count is binomial or Poisson, when a wait is geometric or exponential, and how the normal, gamma, Weibull and log-normal curves differ. After it you can choose a model, write its probability formula, compute probabilities and interpret its mean and variance.
about: The unit starts with counts. Chapter 3.1 builds the binomial distribution from independent trials, and 3.2 takes its rare-event limit to the Poisson distribution. Chapter 3.3 changes the question from a fixed number of trials to waiting for the first or r-th success. The next chapters move to continuous time and measurements: 3.4 gives the flat uniform model, 3.5 gives the exponential wait and its memoryless property, and 3.6 gives the normal bell curve, the standard normal table and normal approximation. Chapter 3.7 closes with skewed positive models—gamma, Weibull and log-normal—used for lifetimes and multiplicative effects. Each chapter keeps formulas tied to mean and variance, so later units on sampling, tests and random processes can use them as building blocks.

chapters.idea: Independent yes/no trials with the same success probability produce the binomial count of successes.
chapters.depth: Cover Bernoulli trials and the binomial probability mass function (pmf) P(X=k)=C(n,k)pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ for n trials, success probability p, k=0,...,n, where C(n,k) is n choose k. Give mean np and variance np(1−p); note symmetry at p=0.5 and the sum of independent binomials with equal p. Some syllabi call it the Bernoulli counting distribution or point binomial. Keep derivations short; use tables or a calculator for C(n,k).

figure.title: Binomial count from ten trials
figure.aria: Four blocks show ten independent UPI trials, counting failures, and applying the binomial pmf with p = 0.2.

chapters.example: A UPI payment fails with probability 0.2 independently. In 10 payments, find P(X = 3) and P(X ≤ 2). Answer: P(X = 3) = 0.2013, P(X ≤ 2) = 0.6778.
chapters.trap: Using binomial when p changes between trials, or forgetting the binomial coefficient; 'at most 2' means k = 0,1,2, not k ≤ 3.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: random variables, expectation and variance; factorials and binomial coefficients.
chapters.leave: Normal approximation to the binomial is in 3.6; large-sample tests for proportions are in Unit 6; MGF derivations are in Unit 2.

chapters.idea: The Poisson distribution counts rare events in a fixed interval when events occur independently at a constant average rate.
chapters.depth: Cover the Poisson pmf P(X=k)=e⁻λ λᵏ/k! for k=0,1,2,... with mean and variance both λ; define λ as mean events per interval. Show the binomial-to-Poisson limit when n is large, p is small and λ=np. Include the additive property for independent Poisson counts and the recurrence. Some syllabi call it the law of rare events. Keep nonhomogeneous and process versions for Unit 7.

figure.aria: Plot of Poisson probabilities for mean four calls per minute, peaking near k = 3 or 4.

chapters.example: A call centre receives on average 4 calls per minute, Poisson. Find P(X=3) and P(X≥2). Answer: P(X=3)=0.1954, P(X≥2)=0.9084.
chapters.trap: Mixing up λ as a rate per minute with λ per five minutes; Poisson counts have no fixed upper limit; mean equals variance is a check, not a proof.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: discrete random variables, expectation, variance; Chapter 3.1 for the binomial limit.
chapters.leave: Poisson process, interarrival times and nonhomogeneous rates are in Unit 7 and Chapter 3.5; tests for Poisson counts are in Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Geometric and negative binomial distributions count trials until the first success or until r successes.
chapters.depth: Cover geometric pmf P(T=k)=(1−p)ᵏ⁻¹p for k=1,2,..., mean 1/p and variance (1−p)/p². Cover negative binomial pmf P(T=k)=C(k−1,r−1)pʳ(1−p)ᵏ⁻ʳ for k=r,r+1,..., mean r/p and variance r(1−p)/p². Show geometric as the r=1 case; state the discrete memoryless property. Some syllabi call negative binomial the Pascal distribution and geometric the waiting-time distribution. Keep only short sums.

figure.title: Waiting for wickets
figure.aria: Flow from independent overs to the geometric first-wicket probability and negative binomial second-wicket probability.

chapters.example: A bowler takes a wicket with probability 0.3 each over, independently. Find P(first wicket in the 4th over) and P(second wicket in the 5th over). Answer: 0.7³ × 0.3 = 0.1029 and C(4,1)0.3²0.7³ = 0.1235.
chapters.trap: Counting failures instead of trials; geometric support starts at 1; negative binomial uses C(k−1,r−1), not C(k,r).
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: discrete random variables, conditional probability; Chapter 3.1 for independent Bernoulli trials.
chapters.leave: Continuous waiting is in 3.5; Markov chain waiting times are in Unit 7.

chapters.idea: The uniform distribution puts equal probability density on every point of a fixed interval.
chapters.depth: Cover the continuous uniform model on [a,b]: probability density function (pdf) f(x)=1/(b−a) for a≤x≤b, CDF F(x)=(x−a)/(b−a), mean (a+b)/2 and variance (b−a)²/12. Show that interval probabilities equal length divided by b−a and that single points have probability zero. Some syllabi call it the rectangular distribution. Keep simulation and random-number generation as a mention only.

figure.aria: A rectangle of height 0.1 from zero to ten minutes shows the uniform density of waiting times.

chapters.example: A metro train runs every 10 minutes, and your arrival time is uniform on (0,10). Let W be your wait in minutes. Find P(W ≤ 3) and E(W). Answer: 0.3 and 5 minutes.
chapters.trap: Using the pdf value 0.1 as a probability; for continuous variables P(W = c) = 0, so ≤ and < are the same.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: continuous random variable, pdf and CDF; basic integration.
chapters.leave: Generating uniform random numbers and simulation are not developed here; normal approximation and central limit are Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The exponential distribution models the wait until the next event in a constant-rate Poisson process and forgets how long you have already waited.
chapters.depth: Cover pdf f(t)=λe⁻λt for t≥0, rate λ>0, mean 1/λ, variance 1/λ², CDF F(t)=1−e⁻λt and survival P(T>t)=e⁻λt. Prove and use memorylessness P(T>s+t | T>s)=P(T>t). Note the discrete analogue in 3.3 and the link to Poisson counts in 3.2. Some syllabi call it the negative exponential distribution. Only a few universities teach the hazard-rate interpretation here; keep it short.

figure.title: Exponential memoryless check
figure.aria: Flow from an exponential lifetime with mean two years to a survival probability and the memoryless conditional equality.

chapters.example: A server component lifetime T is exponential with mean 2 years. Find P(T > 3) and P(T > 5 | T > 3). Answer: e⁻¹·⁵ = 0.2231; by memorylessness P(T > 2) = e⁻¹ = 0.3679.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to convert mean to rate: λ = 1/mean. Memoryless does not mean P(T>5 | T>3)=P(T>5).
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: continuous random variables, pdf, CDF, conditional probability; Chapter 3.3 for the discrete waiting analogue.
chapters.leave: Poisson process, interarrival times and renewal processes are in Unit 7; reliability estimation is in Unit 5 and tests in Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The normal distribution is the symmetric bell curve produced by many small independent errors and used through the standard normal table.
chapters.depth: Cover pdf f(x)=1/(σ√(2π)) exp(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)), mean μ, variance σ², symmetry about μ and the 68–95–99.7 rule. Standardise Z=(X−μ)/σ and use the standard normal table for intervals and inverse problems. Include linear combinations of independent normals and the normal approximation to the binomial with continuity correction. Some syllabi call it the Gaussian distribution. Leave the central limit theorem and multivariate normal to Unit 4.

figure.aria: Bell curve for marks with mean 60 and standard deviation 8, centred at 60.

chapters.example: Exam marks X are normal with mean 60 and standard deviation 8. Find P(50 < X < 70). Answer: z = ±1.25, so the probability is about 0.7887.
chapters.trap: Using σ² in the pdf denominator instead of σ; forgetting continuity correction when approximating a discrete binomial count.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: continuous random variables, expectation, variance; standard normal table; Chapter 3.1 for binomial approximation.
chapters.leave: Central limit theorem and multivariate normal are Unit 4; sampling distributions of mean and variance are Unit 5; normal tests are Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Gamma, Weibull and log-normal are positive skewed families for sums of waits, lifetimes and multiplicative effects.
chapters.depth: Cover definitions and uses: gamma pdf with shape k and rate λ (or scale θ=1/λ), mean k/λ, variance k/λ², and exponential as k=1; Weibull pdf with shape β and scale η, mean ηΓ(1+1/β), hazard increasing or decreasing with β; log-normal when log X is normal, with median e^μ and multiplicative interpretation. Note chi-square is a gamma special case (leave details to Unit 5). Only a few universities teach all three here; some syllabi stop at Weibull. Keep parameter estimation for Unit 5 and goodness of fit for Unit 6.

figure.aria: Three skewed densities on positive time; gamma and log-normal are higher near two, Weibull is lower there.

chapters.example: For Gamma(shape 2, rate 1), Weibull(shape 2, scale 1) and Log-normal(μ=0, σ=0.5), compare the densities at t=2 and state which is largest. Answer: gamma 0.2707, Weibull 0.0733, log-normal 0.1520; gamma is largest.
chapters.trap: Calling log-normal 'the log of a normal'; it is the distribution of X when log X is normal. Mixing rate and scale in gamma or Weibull.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: continuous random variables, pdf, integration; Chapter 3.5 for exponential as a gamma special case; gamma function Γ(·).
chapters.leave: Chi-square distribution and tests are Unit 5 and Unit 6; parameter estimation is Unit 5; reliability and acceptance sampling applications are outside this unit.
